title: Meeting Louis Armstrong again; Barney Bigard in his band
summary: Charles tells of finding Armstrong at his hotel and attending the concert, and says Bigard played clarinet and sax with him.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Do you remember little dad? Dad. The banjo player, he was just about deaf probably about that time. Little short, short fella. He's passed on, but he told me about you a couple of years ago. I'm sure I must know.

Because like I tell you, there was one you could name that I didn't know. Because like I tell you, if they could play or they didn't play, that was my friend. What did he say? We lived. We lived. I'm telling you Armstrong, I hadn't seen Armstrong for so long until I thought, I'd not forget about him. But I was looking in the showcase at the App Dallas and somebody told me, another white fellow was there looking at the showcase too. And so we talked, talked, talked, and first thing you know, was looking at, do you remember how they generally put swords, all kinds of soldiers thing in the showcase at the App Dallas? That's right. He told me, he said, they got a musician. I told him, I said, I was a musician once. When he said something, but I happened to tell him I was a musician. So when he said, I got a musician talking to Mr. Hyman right now in the Hyman store. I said, what's his name? He said, Lewis Armstrong. Oh, I said, my goodness. I said, brother, we ain't talking no more. I said, let me go there and see Lewis. So I went in the store to see Lewis, but Lewis had done gone to the hotel. The clerk took me all around to try to find him, but them cultural folks that see me back there all the time, he said, no, Lewis going home, going to the hotel. I said, well, all right. Where's the hotel? They told me where the hotel was and I went to the hotel. So Lewis told me when I got there, I told the manager of the hotel, I said, Lewis Armstrong here? He said, yes. He hollered, oh, Lewis, somebody want to see you. Tell him, he was like, come on down, boy. Come on down, don't burn you. And I went upstairs there and there he played a whole lot of little machine like that too. He did. So he wanted me to know what he did, you know. So after he got through, he said, you've got to come hear me, I'm playing at SLR. He said, we've got a concert there. Come in here to the concert. I can't give you some, you pass. You don't have to worry about it. And then he did it too. And I went there, I rushed up here and I closed the stove, dressed myself and I went up there. And believe me, he had a nice band. He sure did. Yeah, a nice band. And then right after the concert, you know, they go downstairs there. And then I had to go there with them, you see, and asked me. I couldn't leave him. We must have shook him about four or five times. Him and Bonnie Biggar, because Bonnie used to play with me, you see. Well, won't you come play with me, good boy? I said, oh no, we can't do anything now. What bands did you play with? Louis never did play with you. He used to come hear us play, but never did play with you. Is that right? He didn't play parades with him? No. Louis was just coming out. Oh I see. Oh yeah. Bonnie Biggar, he was a band. He was a band. He was a band.
He was a band. He was a band. He was a band. He was a band. He was a band. He was a band.
He was a band. He was a band. He was a band. He was a band. You didn't play parades with him? No. Lou was just coming out. Oh I see.
Barney Biggar played with me a long time.
In your own band? Oh yeah, my own band. What was he playing, clarinet or sax?
And both of them? Oh yeah. Which was he the best of them? I always wondered about that. Sax or clarinet then?
Well I tell you I'd rather hear Barney on the clarinet than anything else. Oh yeah, now? Oh believe me. That boy can play that clarinet.
